findings.text: — the Why asserts the release step records the `release` block "only in the ledger file ... never the run store", but `reckon/crew/promotion_release.py:803` amends the run file through `ledger.write_run_file`, which calls `_sync_amended_run` (`reckon/ledger.py:959`) and therefore `run_store.sync`; two runs released on 2026-11-17 (`r-20261117T210129316927-plan-review-of-history-persists-as-detail-washes-out`, `r-20261117T211344061865-plan-review-of-delivered-work-lands-without-a-coordinator`) read back through `stored_run_rows` with a `release` block byte-equal to their run files.

— the first arm is declared "failing at the base revision", but at the base revision a promoted run that owns a per-run file already answers its `release` block from the store, so that arm is green at base and measures nothing; the only path still red at base is a release written through the aggregate ledger file, which does not sync rows, and the seven store rows measured as lacking release are all releases recorded before `4f04392824` (2026-11-16) added that sync.

— f-hpdw-015's resolved outcome ends "§27 is next", but s27's only declared upstream is s26 (`plan.html:29`), s26 is still `implementable` (`plan.html:28`), and the open followup f-hpdw-017 (plan.html:536) queues §36 and then §26's merge repair, so the record points a dispatcher at a node whose upstream has not landed.

response_events.note: s36's Why now states the measured cause: per-run releases have synced to the store since 4f04392824, and the 8 differing rows are releases recorded before that sync
